activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
knowledge_domain: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Claire was at Grandma's house. She wanted to play house with her teddy bear. But teddy was missing. She looked under the big chair. She looked behind the door. No teddy.

Grandma sat down beside her. "Let's make a bed for teddy," Grandma said. "Then teddy will want to come home." So Claire got a small box. She put in a soft sock. She laid a tissue on top, like a little blanket.

Then Claire heard a funny sound. Peep, peep! It came from the last basket on the shelf. Claire stood on her toes. There was teddy! A bird was singing a song outside the window, and teddy had been hiding near the sound. "The song brought the bird," Claire said. "The bird woke teddy up!" Claire put teddy in the new bed. She patted his head. "Night night, teddy," she said. Grandma smiled and turned off the little lamp.

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
knowledge_domain: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Isaac jumped into the family car. He wanted his little blue dinosaur. But the dinosaur was not in his bag. Oh no! Where did it go?

"Last look!" said Mom. "We have to go now." Isaac sat in his seat. Then he remembered something. He had hugged the dinosaur when the car turned fast. The car had gone round the big corner. Everything slid to one side. Maybe the dinosaur slid too!

Isaac bent down low. He peeked under his seat. He saw a shoe. He saw a cracker. No dinosaur yet. He looked on the other side. He reached his hand way down. His fingers touched something bumpy. Something little. Something blue!

"I found him!" Isaac shouted. He pulled the dinosaur up high. "He slid under the seat when the car turned!" Mom laughed and clapped. The car began to go. Isaac hugged his dinosaur tight. "Soon we will be home," he said. "Then we can have a snack in the kitchen!" He spun the dinosaur around and around until he felt dizzy. The dinosaur got a big kiss right on his nose.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Natalie was in her playroom. She wanted to paint a green frog. But where was the green paint?

She looked in her paint box. She found red. She found blue. She found yellow. No green at all.

"Oh no," said Natalie. "My frog needs green."

She was hungry for her snack, but the frog came first. Natalie squeezed some blue paint. She squeezed some yellow paint too. She dipped her brush in both colors. She stirred them round and round on the paper.

The paint turned green! "Look at that!" said Natalie. Blue and yellow made green. She said it out loud: "Blue and yellow make green. That is why!"

She filled the whole page with green. Then she painted the frog's big eyes. She painted its little nose, right on its face.

"Mama, come see!" she called. "My frog is green!"

Mama came in and smiled. Natalie held up the painting.

"I made green all by myself," said Natalie. "Now can I have my snack?"

activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
knowledge_domain: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
story:
Margot wanted to draw a winter picture at school. She wanted a hill and a hat and big white snow. She picked up the tablet. She tapped the screen once. The screen stayed dark. She tapped it again. Still dark. She asked her teacher, "Why won't it wake up?"

Her teacher said, "Try the little round button. Hold it down."

Margot found the round button on the side. She pressed it with her finger. She held it and held it. Then the screen lit up. "The button makes it go," said Margot. "Tap does nothing. Hold makes it start."

She found the drawing app. It had a rainbow on it. She drew a white hill and a red hat and lots of snow. Then the timer rang. Play time was done. Margot pressed the button again. The screen asked, "Turn off?" She tapped yes. The screen went dark. She put the tablet back on the shelf, flat and neat.

"You put it away all by yourself," said her teacher. "That is a win."

Margot smiled at the shelf. "The tablet sleeps there now," she said.

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
knowledge_domain: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story: Wesley was a small boy. He walked in the forest with his bear, Blue. Blue was hungry. Wesley had no spoon for pretend soup. He looked on the ground. He found a smooth brown stick. "This can be your spoon," he said. He stirred leaves in a little puddle. The stick made the soup. "Eat it all up," he said. Blue ate and ate. Then Wesley carried Blue to a mossy log. "This is our house now," he said. First they ate soup. Then they had a nap. A soft wind blew. The leaves went swish, swish. Wesley covered Blue with a big green leaf. "Good night, Blue," he said. "Sleep tight in our house." The forest went quiet and still.

activity: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
knowledge_domain: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
story:
Gabriella sat on a small chair in Miss Polly's music room. Miss Polly played a song on the piano. "Now we clap," she said. Gabriella clapped fast, fast, fast. The claps did not match the song. Her hands felt mixed up. She wanted to hide them under her legs.

Miss Polly stopped playing. She patted Gabriella's back. "Try again, little one," she said. "Listen first." Miss Polly played the slow beat. One, two, one, two. Gabriella listened. Then she clapped one, two, one, two. Her hands landed right on the beat. "My claps go with the song!" she said. "The claps are slow like the music."

"Now let's sing," said Miss Polly. They sang "Baa, Baa, Black Sheep" together. Then Miss Polly went quiet. Gabriella sang it all by herself. She remembered every word. On the wall was a picture of a small sheep with a woolly coat. Miss Polly clapped for her. "One more song?" she asked. "Yes!" said Gabriella, and she began to sing.

activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
knowledge_domain: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Hazel went to the library with her dad. She wanted the book with the big red chicken on it. But she could not reach the shelf. It was too high.

A lady with a blue cardigan walked by. Hazel pulled her sleeve and said, "Book!" The lady did not move. Hazel tried again. "Book, please." The lady smiled. "Ah, you want the chicken book! Here you go." Her bag began to swing as she reached up high.

Hazel looked at the book. "Please got the book," she said. Her dad nodded. "Please helps people hear you."

On the way out, Hazel bumped into a boy. "Sorry," she said. He said, "That's okay." At the desk, the lady gave her a stamp on a fresh card. "Thank you," said Hazel. The lady gave her a big thumbs up. "Come back soon, Hazel!"

activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
knowledge_domain: people's jobs and how a community works
fact: At a library, you can borrow books and take them home, but you must bring them back by a certain day so other people can read them too.
story:
Logan stood at the big library desk. He wanted a book about trucks. The librarian gave him a card with his name on it. "Your very first card," she said. Logan held it with both hands.

He found a truck book on a low shelf. He sat on the floor and looked at the pictures. The wheels looked big and shiny. He smelled the pages. They smelled like paper and old rain.

"I want to keep it," Logan told his mom. "Forever and ever."

"You can take it home," Mom said. "But a stamp inside says when to bring it back. Other kids want to read it too."

Logan looked at the stamp. He put the book under his arm. His loose tooth wiggled when he smiled.

At home he read the book on his knee. Every night he turned the pages. Then the day came. The stamp day.

Logan carried the book back to the library. He set it on the desk. "I brought it back," he said. "Now another kid can read it."

The librarian smiled. "That was kind. And you can borrow it again."

Logan's tooth felt even looser. He picked a new book about cranes. "Thank you," he said to the librarian. He held his card tight all the way home.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: people's jobs and how a community works
fact: At a library, you can borrow books and take them home, but you must bring them back by a certain day so other people can read them too.
story:
Emily was at Grandma's house. She found a big book on the sofa. The book had little marks on every page. Grandma called the marks words. "The words tell the story," said Grandma. Grandma opened the front of the book. Then she turned the pages one by one. The story went from the front to the back.

"I want this book forever," said Emily. She hugged it tight. Grandma said, "The book is from the library. We can take it home. But we must bring it back by Saturday. Then other people can read it too." Emily held the book. She did not want to let it go.

They read the book together. It was about a green frog. The frog sat on a log by a pond. The frog was slimy and cool. In the garden, Emily bent down to see a real worm. She looked so long that her neck began to hurt. Grandma rubbed her neck softly. "The worm is slimy too," said Emily. "It is, little one," said Grandma.

On Saturday, they walked to the library. Emily gave the book to the lady at the desk. "You brought it back," the lady said. "Now someone else can read it." Emily looked at the book on the shelf. Then she picked a new one. She opened the front page first. "New words," said Emily. Grandma smiled and took her hand.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Dylan wanted a snack. He saw the big pot on the stove. Steam went up from the pot. "Hot," said Mama. "The pot can hurt you."

Dylan put his hand near the pot. The air felt warm. He pulled his hand back fast. He did not touch the pot. "The pot is hot because it is on the fire," Dylan said. Mama smiled and gave him a cold apple slice instead. It felt cool in his hand.

Then Dylan wanted to go outside. He ran to the door. But he stopped and looked back. Mama was still in the kitchen. "Stay close to me," said Mama. So Dylan held her hand. They went outside together.

Dylan saw a shiny tool on the grass. It had sharp teeth. He did not touch it. "Mama, this is not for kids," he said. Mama put it away high on a shelf. Then they sat on the steps. Dylan bit his apple. It went crunch. "Crunchy," he said with a big smile.

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
knowledge_domain: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Stella loved the little kitchen at school. Today the baby doll would not stop crying. Stella held her close. "Why is Baby crying?" she asked. Then she saw it. Baby's arm had a big scratch.

Stella laid Baby on the table. She got a soft cloth. She patted the scratch, very gently. But Baby still cried.

Then Ben came over. "I can be the doctor," he said. He picked up a toy phone. "Ring, ring," he said. "Hello, Doctor? Baby has a scratch." He listened to the phone. Then he nodded. "The Doctor says she needs a bandage."

Stella found a sticker bandage. She stuck it on Baby's arm. She wrapped Baby in a small blanket. She gave her pretend milk from a tiny cup.

Baby stopped crying. Stella smiled big. "She is better now," she said. "We called the Doctor, and the Doctor helped."

Ben grinned. "You are a lucky mom," he said. "Your Baby has a bandage now."

Stella rocked Baby in her arms. "Shh, shh," she sang. "Time to sleep, little one." Baby's eyes closed, just like that.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
story:
Zoey found a big drum in the garage. It sat on a wooden stand. The wood was old and dusty.

She tapped the drum. It went boom. It sounded low and floppy. Zoey wanted a happy sound. She tapped it again. Still floppy.

Dad came in. He was not mean. He was kind. He gave her a small key. "The drum needs tight skin," he said. "Try turning this."

Zoey turned the key. She turned it a lot. The skin got tight. She tapped the drum. Ting! Now it sounded high and clean.

"Dad! Tight skin makes a good sound," she said. "Loose skin makes a floppy sound."

She tapped it fast. Ting, ting, ting. Dad tapped his knees. They played a song together.

activity: starting the first day of school
knowledge_domain: starting the first day of school
story:
Sienna stood at the gate. The playground was big. She held her mama's hand tight.

"Go on," said Mama. "Your teacher will call your name." Sienna walked to the sand table. She found a cup of water. She stirred it fast with a stick. Bubbles came up in the air. They popped one by one.

A boy came close. He looked at her shirt. There was a red tag on it. The tag had letters. "Sienna," he read out loud. "Hi, Sienna. I am Leo."

Sienna looked down at her tag. "You know my name," she said. "The tag tells you."

"Yes," said Leo. "That is what tags are for."

At the paint table, Leo mixed blue and yellow. The paint turned green. Sienna gasped. "It changed," she said. She made green too, with her own stick.

Then it was time for bubbles. The teacher blew thin, shiny bubbles. One landed on Sienna's shoe. It did not pop. It sat there like a little window.

"Look, Leo," said Sienna. "A bubble on my shoe."

Leo sat down next to her. "First days are fun," he said.

Sienna smiled at her red tag. "My name helped," she said. "It found me a friend."

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Adam sat at the little red table. Ten apple slices sat on his plate. He wanted to count them all.

"One, two, five," said Adam. His friend Mia frowned. "That is not the song," she said. Adam sang the counting song in his head. "One, two, three, four, five." The numbers came out in a row.

He tried again. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Ten apple slices! He touched each slice as he said a number. "Why did it work?" he asked. "I said them in the song order," he said.

Mia dropped her apple on the floor. Adam picked it up. Then he gave her one of his fresh slices. She took a big bite and smiled.

Outside, Adam found a leaf on the ground. He counted it. "One leaf." Then he found another. "One, two." Mia laughed. "You count everything," she said.

"Ten," said Adam. "Count with me."

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
Grandma's big TV was on. It was game night at Grandma's house. Georgia sat on the floor with her blanket.

Everyone watched the game. Aunts and uncles and cousins came too. Georgia wanted to see the ball. But the couch was big. The grown-ups were big too.

Then the team ran fast. The people on TV scored a point. Everyone jumped up. "Hooray!" they shouted. Everyone stood in front of Georgia. She could not see the TV at all. Georgia sat very still. She waited.

Soon the game went on. Everyone sat back down. Georgia could see the TV again. Then the team scored another point. Everyone jumped up again. "Hooray!" they shouted. Georgia could not see again.

Georgia thought and thought. When the people scored, everyone stood up. When they did not score, everyone sat down. So she got her little stool. She stood on the stool by the couch. Now she could see over everyone.

The team scored again. Everyone jumped up. But Georgia was up high on her stool. She could see the ball go in. She could see the striped shirts running on the green grass. "I see it! I see it!" she said.

Grandma looked at her and smiled. "Look at Georgia," said Grandma. "She waited and found a good spot." The game went on and on into the night. Georgia stood on her stool the whole time. When the last point came, she shouted with everyone. "Hooray!"

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story: Rehmat lost her red ball in the backyard. "Ball, ball!" she called out loud. She heard a dog bark with her ears. The sound came from behind the big rock. Rehmat looked with her eyes. She saw the shiny ball on top of the rock, like a little red mountain. It was too high to reach. Rehmat closed her eyes and grabbed. She touched only leaves. "I cannot see," she said. "So my hands miss." She opened her eyes again. Now her hands found the ball. A smell came to her nose. It was sweet. Mom was cutting a mango at the table. Rehmat ran to her. Mom gave her a slice. Rehmat tasted it with her tongue. "Sweet!" she said. Then she shared one piece with the dog."Come here, boy!" she called. "This is for you."

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
knowledge_domain: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Colton went to the store with Mom. He held his bunny. Then he let go to grab an apple. Bunny was gone. "Bunny is lost," Colton said. "Bunny is lost."

Mom knelt down. "Let's draw a picture of Bunny," she said. Mom drew a picture on her list. Bunny had long ears. Mom showed the picture to a worker. The worker smiled. "I will help you look," she said.

Then Colton had an idea. He went back to the apples. He looked where his feet had been. "Bunny fell here," he said. "Bunny fell because I let go." There was Bunny, on the floor by the apples!

Colton hugged Bunny tight. The worker clapped. Mom said, "You found Bunny because you went back to the same spot." On the way home, Colton drew a big bunny picture for his teacher. "Bunny is found," he said. "Found, found, found."

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Leo went to the park with Mom. He wanted to find the red ball. He held Mom's hand on the way. "Stay close to me," said Mom. Leo stayed close to Mom.

The sun made the slide very hot. Leo put his hand near it. "Ouch, hot!" he said. He pulled his hand back fast. The slide was too hot to touch. So Leo sat in the shade instead. The shade felt cool and nice.

Then Leo saw something shiny near the fence. It was a rough old can with sharp edges. Leo wanted to kick it. But he stopped. Sharp things can hurt you. Leo did not touch it. He ran back to Mom. "I did not touch the sharp can," he said. Mom smiled and patted his head.

Leo found his red ball by the tree. He kicked the ball to Mom. Mom kicked it back. Leo laughed and held his tummy. "The slide was hot because the sun was on it," said Leo. Mom nodded. "Yes, little one. The sun makes things hot." Leo kicked the ball again, far and high.

activity: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
knowledge_domain: counting, comparing amounts, and shapes
fact: When you count a group of things, the last number you say tells how many there are. You get the same answer no matter which one you count first.
story:
Peyton sat at the big table in math club. There were two plates of cookies. The sweet smell made her tummy giggle. "We can each pick a plate," said her friend Ben.

Peyton wanted more cookies. But which plate had more? She counted the red plate. She started at the left end. "One, two, three, four, five." Then she counted again, from the right end. "One, two, three, four, five." The last number was the same!

Ben laughed. "You counted them twice, silly."

"I had to check," said Peyton. "The end number is still five. It does not care where I start."

The blue plate had four. Peyton picked the red plate. "Five is more than four. More cookies for me!"

Ben giggled and picked the last one.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story: Amira stood at the little table in the cooking classroom. Today she would make bread for her family. She mixed flour, water and yeast in a big bowl. Then she patted the dough flat like a pancake. "Now we wait," said Teacher Jo. "Why?" asked Amira. "You will see," said Teacher Jo, and she smiled. Amira waited. She watched. The dough got puffy. It grew big and fat. Amira put her hand on it. It felt soft, like a sheep's wool. "The yeast makes little bubbles," Amira said. "The bubbles push the bread up." She shaped the dough into a nice round loaf. Her friend Ben dropped his spoon. Amira picked it up for him. "Thank you," said Ben. The teacher put the loaf in the oven. Soon the whole room smelled warm and sweet. Amira carried the bread home in a basket. "I made this," she said. "It is big because the bubbles pushed it up." Her family ate it all up.

activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
knowledge_domain: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
story:
Brielle sat in the nursery. A little bed was by the sun. In the bed was her new baby brother. He was so cute.

Brielle was happy. She wanted to clap. She clapped her hands. Clap, clap! The baby woke up. He began to cry. "Waa, waa," he said.

Mom came in. She held her finger to her lips. "Shh," said Mom. "The baby was sleeping. He woke up because it was too loud."

Brielle nodded. She sat very still. She counted the baby's toes. "One, two, three," she whispered. "Four, five." The baby stopped crying. He closed his eyes. He went back to sleep.

"He sleeps because it is quiet," Brielle whispered. Mom smiled and kissed her head. Brielle looked at her brother. "I will clap tomorrow," she whispered.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Bennett ran into the backyard. He wanted to find his red ball. He looked by the tall fence. He looked under the big tree.

Then he heard a sound. Sizzle, sizzle. It came from the grill. "Dad, what is that?" he asked. "The grill is hot," Dad said. "It can hurt your hand. Do not touch it."

Bennett stepped back. He put his hand near the grill from far away. He felt warm air. "The fire makes it hot," he said. "That is why it sizzles."

Just then he saw his red ball. It sat close to the grill. "Dad, my ball is there!" Dad picked it up with the long tongs. He held it out. "Here you are. Stay close to me and play here."

Bennett hugged the ball. "Thank you, Dad." He rolled it on the cool grass.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
story:
Sebastian went to the library with his mom. There was a craft table by the window. On the table were red paper, blue paper, and a big jar of glue. "I will make a fish," said Sebastian. He drew a fish with one fin, two fins, three fins. Then he wanted to put the paper fish on a big blue sheet. He dug in the craft bin for a spoon. He found one. He scooped a lot of glue. He spread it all over the blue paper. It was wet and shiny. He pressed his fish down.

The fish stuck. But the blue paper got bumpy. Little hills grew all around the fish. The paper had been smooth. Now it was not. Sebastian touched the hills with his finger. "Too much glue," he said. "The paper got all wet. That made the bumps."

A girl next to him was gluing too. She used one little dot of glue. Her paper stayed smooth. Sebastian got a new blue sheet. He made one dot. Then two dots. Then three dots. He pressed the fish down. The paper stayed flat and smooth. He held it up to the window. The sun made the red fish glow. "Mom, look!" he said. "One dot is enough. My fish is flat and happy." At home in the kitchen, his mom put the fish on the fridge with a magnet.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
knowledge_domain: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Jules sat at the dinner table. His tooth felt loose. He wiggled it with his tongue. Then he heard a sound. His sister Mia was crying. Her face looked sad. Jules knew sad faces. Sad faces have a turned-down mouth.

Why was Mia sad? He looked near her plate. Her potato had rolled off. It sat on the floor. "Did your potato go away?" he asked. Mia nodded. "Yes. I want it back."

Jules got down from his chair. He picked up the potato. He washed it at the sink. Then he put it back on her plate. Mia's mouth turned up. Now her face looked happy. Jules felt happy too. His heart went bump, bump, bump with excitement.

"You made me smile," said Mia. "I saw your sad face," said Jules. "So I helped." He wiggled his loose tooth again. It felt funny. He was a little scared it might fall out. But Mama sat near him. She held his hand. His scared feeling got small and small. Then Daddy said, "Ice cream for dessert!" Jules jumped. "Yay!" he said. His voice was loud and excited. Excited voices go up, up, up.

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
story:
Grandpa came on the big train. Noah ran to meet him on the platform. Grandpa had a red bag and a big smile.

"I will stay for seven whole days," said Grandpa. "A week has seven days." Noah made a paper chain. It had seven paper rings. One ring for each day.

But Grandpa looked sad at supper. "I miss my tea at home," he said. Noah got the teapot. The teabag went into the bowl of hot water. It sat and sat. Then the water turned brown. "The tea makes the water brown," said Noah. "I see why now!" Grandpa laughed. "You got it, Noah." The first tea was too weak. The second cup was just right. "The first one was wrong because I took the bag out too fast," said Noah. The paper chain sank down in Grandpa's tea, but Noah dried it with a towel.

Each night, Noah took one ring off the chain. Six rings. Then five. Then one. On the last morning, one ring was left. "Last day!" said Noah. He held Grandpa's hand at the station. "Come back soon," said Noah. "I will make your tea just right."

activity: starting the first day of school
knowledge_domain: starting the first day of school
story:
Sadie stood in the new school hallway. She held her paper boat tight. The boat had a sail and a little flag. Her tummy felt funny.

A big door opened. Kids ran out to play. Sadie did not know where to go. She looked down the hall. So many doors! She held her boat closer.

A kind teacher stopped by her. "Where is your tag?" the teacher asked. Sadie looked. A tag was on her coat! It had her name on it. The teacher read the tag. "Sadie! Your class is this way."

The tag told the teacher her name. That is why the teacher knew her! Sadie smiled big.

In the class room, there was a water table. Sadie put her boat in. She stirred the water with her hand. The boat sailed round and round. The water made it move!

"My boat can sail here," Sadie said.

activity: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
knowledge_domain: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
story:
Levi wanted to paint a dragon egg. A big, green dragon egg. But the paint pots had no green.

Levi looked at the pots. "Red, yellow, blue," he said. "Red, yellow, blue." He said it again, like a magic spell. The teacher painted a thin line of blue on his paper. Then she painted a yellow line right on top of it.

Levi leaned close. The lines touched. They wiggled. They turned green! "It's a magic egg color!" he said. He dipped his brush in blue, then in yellow, and mixed them in his tray. Green, green, wonderful green. He painted a big round egg. He painted it all over, top to bottom.

When he finished, the egg was so green it seemed to glow. A dragon lived in there, Levi was sure of it. He held the paper up to his ear and listened. "I hear it tapping," he whispered. "It wants to say hello."

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
knowledge_domain: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
story:
Everett ran to the swings. The sky was cloudy, but he did not mind. "One, two, three, up to the tree!" he shouted. The swing made him feel like a bird.

But the swings were full. A girl was on one. A boy was on the other. Everett wanted a swing so much. He stood and waited. Then he waited more.

The girl jumped off. "Your turn," she said. "You waited, so you go next." Everett got on the swing. His tummy felt like jelly. "Wee!" he cried. "Up to the tree!"

Then the boy said, "My turn again." Everett held the chains tight. He looked at the boy's face. The boy looked sad. Everett remembered waiting. Waiting was long. "Okay," said Everett. "You waited, so you go next." He hopped off. The boy smiled big.

Later they all played in the wood chips. "Let's cook a cake!" said Everett. They stirred leaves in a bucket. Each friend added one leaf. "One for me, one for you," said Everett. "One for me, one for you." The cake had a bit from everyone.

The bell rang. Time to go. Everett held the gate and counted friends going out. One, two, three. "All out!" he said. Then he ran to his mom, still holding one leafy cake piece. "Can we cook a real cake at home?" he asked.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Wyatt wanted to help Dad in the backyard. Dad was cooking soup on a little stove. "Stay close to me," Dad said. Wyatt stayed close to Dad.

The pot made a hiss. Steam went up, up, up. Wyatt put his hand near it. The air felt hot, not cold. He pulled his hand back fast. "Hot air," he said. "I will not touch the pot." Dad nodded.

Wyatt saw a shiny tool on the grass. It was sharp and wet from the sprinkler. He did not touch it. "Sharp tools can hurt," he said. Dad put it away high on a shelf.

Then Dad poured cold milk into a small cup. Wyatt took a little taste. "Yum," said Wyatt. "The milk is cold. The pot is hot. I stay close to you." Dad smiled and held his hand. "Good helper," said Dad. "Good helper."

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Margot sat down at the dinner table. She had ten peas on her plate. "I can count them," she said. "One, two, three, five, eight, ten!" Dad smiled. "Ten peas? Let's look again."

Margot poked the peas with her spoon. She counted slow this time. "One, two, three, four." The peas kept going. "Five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." All the peas had a number. "Where did four go before?" she asked. "Maybe I jumped over it."

"You did jump," said Dad. "The numbers have an order. One comes before two." Margot tapped her spoon on the table. Tap, tap, tap. "One, two, three," she sang, like the song at school.

Then she held up her milk cup. It had a big owl on it. "Mr. Owl can count too," she said. "I pretend he is the counting teacher." She made a low owl voice. "Hoo, hoo. One, two, three." Margot laughed. "Owls are not scary at all," she said. "Not when they count."

She looked at Dad's plate. He had peas too. "Can I count yours?" she asked. Dad pushed his plate close. Margot pointed at each green pea. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Dad clapped. Margot ate a pea. Now she would count nine. She grinned and tapped the cup again. "Hoo," said Mr. Owl. "One, two, three."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Matthew put on his big red apron. "I wear my apron like a chef," he said. Dad smiled. "Let's buy food for dinner," said Dad. They walked to the farmers' market.

At the market, Matthew saw a shiny fish on the ice. "It looks like silver," he said. Dad said, "Yes. We can cook that fish for dinner." Matthew carried the bag. It was cold and heavy.

At home, Dad put a pan on the stove. "Hot pan, careful hands," said Dad. Matthew said it too. "Hot pan, careful hands." Then Dad put butter in the pan. Matthew watched. The butter was hard. Then the pan got hot. The hard butter turned to liquid and slid around. Matthew jumped a little. "The butter is all runny!" he said. "Why did it do that?" Dad said, "You tell me." Matthew thought. Then he said, "The pan is hot. Hot makes the butter melt." Dad said, "That's right. Heat melts butter."

Matthew helped put the shiny fish in the melted butter. It went sizzle, sizzle. He held Dad's hand and stayed back a step. Soon the fish smelled good. Mom came in and said, "Mmm, who is the chef?" Matthew held up his red apron. "I am!" he said. They all sat down. The fish was warm and soft. Matthew took a big bite and said, "Hot pan, careful hands, good fish!"

activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
knowledge_domain: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
story:
James was at Grandma's house. It was cold outside. Grandma said, "Time for the park."

James grabbed his red coat. He pushed one arm in. Then the other arm. "I can do it," he said.

Now for the zipper. James pulled it up. It stopped right away. He pulled again. It would not move. James made a sad face. "The zipper is broken," he said.

Grandma knelt down beside him. "Look at the bottom," she said softly. James looked. His coat edge was stuck in the zipper. That is why it would not go up. James pulled the cloth out. He held it away with one hand. He pulled the zipper with his other hand. Zip! It went all the way up.

"It was the cloth," said James. "The cloth was in the way."

Grandma smiled. "Yes, it was. You fixed it all by yourself." James felt very big. He ran to the door. "Let's go, Grandma! I want my sandwich at the park. All this zipping made me hungry and thirsty too."

Grandma laughed and picked up the little bag. James zipped his coat again, just to hear the sound. Zip! Zip!

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
knowledge_domain: spending a surprise snow day at home
story:
Chloe woke up early. She looked out the window. Snow! White snow was on the grass. "No school today," said Mom. "It is a snow day!" Chloe laughed and jumped on her bed.

Chloe ran to the backyard. The snow was cold on her boots. It crunched under her feet. But the steps were slippery. Mom slipped a little. "Oh no," said Mom. "Be careful, Chloe."

Chloe had an idea. Dad kept a big bag of salt by the door. Dad put salt on the steps. "Watch now," he said. Chloe waited. Drip, drip, drip. Little holes opened in the ice. The salt was melting it! "The salt makes the ice go away," said Chloe. She put more salt on the path with her little cup. Drip, drip. Soon the steps were safe.

The mail truck came down the street. Chloe ran to the mailbox. A letter was inside! Mom read it to her. It was from Grandma. Chloe held the warm letter in her mittens. "Look, Grandma made a snowman on the paper," she said. "I will draw her one back."

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Avery sat in her car seat. The seat belt clicked. "Are we there now?" she asked. "Not yet," said Mama. "We will get there later." Avery looked out the window. A thin cloud slid by. "Where does the cloud go now?" she asked.

Mama smiled. "The cloud goes this way now. It went that way yesterday too." Avery pressed her ear to the window. She heard the road go rumbly rumbly. Yesterday the road had been quiet. Why? Then she saw why. Today the road was wet. The rain had come yesterday. Wet wheels made the big sound. "The rain made the road loud!" she said. "The rain came yesterday, and now the wheels go rumbly."

"What do we do at Grandma's house?" asked Avery. "We will bake cookies later," said Mama. "Today?" asked Avery. "Yes, today," said Mama. "And tomorrow we eat them again." Avery clapped her hands. The rain had come yesterday. The cookies would come later. Today was the car day, and the wheels went rumbly rumbly all the way.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Nova went to the park with her blue bag. "The ducks were here yesterday," said Nova. "Ducks are here today, too." She threw a small piece of bread. One duck ate it fast. That was funny.

"Now I want to ride the swing," said Nova. But a boy was on the swing. "You can ride later," said Mom. Nova waited. She sat on the bench. She looked at the ducks some more. Waiting was slow, but that was okay.

The boy jumped off the swing. "It is later now!" said Nova. She ran to the swing. Mom pushed her up high. "The sun is going down," said Mom. "We can come back tomorrow." Nova kissed Mom's cheek. "Tomorrow, ducks," said Nova, waving her bag.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: people's jobs and how a community works
fact: At a library, you can borrow books and take them home, but you must bring them back by a certain day so other people can read them too.
story:
Matteo had a library book. It was about a red truck. He held it in his lap. He opened the front cover first. "This is the start," said Mama. Matteo pointed at the little marks on the page. "What is that?" he asked. "Those are words," said Mama. "They say truck goes up the hill." Matteo looked at the words. Then he looked at the truck. The words told about the truck!

Matteo loved the red truck book. He wanted to keep it forever. But then Mama said, "Library day is tomorrow. We take the book back." Matteo held the book tight. "My book," he said. His tummy felt tight, like a little problem was sitting in it. "Other kids want to read it too," said Mama. "Someone else will borrow it, just like we did."

The next day, Matteo put the book in his bag. He popped the bag on his back. At the library, he set the book on the big desk. A lady smiled and said, "Thank you." Then Matteo found a shelf of new books. He picked one about a fresh yellow banana. He opened the front cover. The words were there, waiting for him. "We take this one home," he said. "And bring it back next time." Mama nodded. "Yes. Just like that." Matteo hugged the new book all the way home.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
Rose sat in a big red seat. Dad sat on her left. Grandma sat on her right. The game was down on the green grass. It was so far away.

A spotted dog walked by with a man. Then something strange began. One row of people stood up. They threw their arms up high. Then they sat down. The next row stood up. Then the next one. It came closer and closer. Dad stood up. He put his arms up. Rose stayed in her seat. She missed it. The row behind her stood. Rose turned to look. Too late again.

Rose watched and watched. The far rows stood first. Then the near rows. She saw why. Each row waited for the row in front. Now it was coming back. It was almost at Dad. Rose planted her feet on the floor. She stood up tall. Up went her arms. Down she sat, just in time. Grandma laughed and clapped. "Again," said Rose. "Watch the front row." The wave came around once more. This time Rose stood up with everyone, right on time.

activity: starting the first day of school
knowledge_domain: starting the first day of school
story:
Max climbed the big yellow school bus. He held his backpack tight. He wanted to sit with his friend Sam.

Max looked at all the seats. Where was Sam? Max walked down the aisle. The bus floor bounced under his feet.

Then Max saw the bus window. Sam was on the other side of it! Sam had not gotten on the bus yet. Max waved through the glass. Sam waved back and climbed the steps.

Sam sat down next to Max. "You were outside the window," Max said. "That is why I could not find you!"

Sam laughed. He opened his lunch box. He shared a sweet red apple with Max.

The bus started to roll. Max looked out the window. The trees went by, then his school.

"That is where we learn," said Sam. "My big sister will teach us the song."

Max smiled and took another big bite.

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Sienna went to the store with Dad. She wanted apples for a song. "We need apples to sing," she said.

Dad put one apple in the bag. Then two apples. Sienna tapped the bag. "One, two, seven, ten!" she said. Dad smiled. "Let's try again, slow and easy." He tapped the bag with her. "One, two, three." Sienna watched his finger. The words came in a row, like steps on stairs.

A man in a green hat walked by. He had a messy cart full of bread. He hummed a song. "One, two, three, four, five," he sang. Sienna listened. His words were the same as Dad's words, in the same order.

Sienna counted the apples again. "One, two, three, four, five." She got them all in the right row this time. She waited, then tried once more. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten."

"Ten apples!" said Dad. Sienna put the bag in the cart. The numbers went in a line, so she sang them in a line. She did a little dance by the apples. The man in the green hat waved. "Nice counting," he said.

At home, Sienna held up the bag. "Ten apples, Grandma! Want to sing with me?"

activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
knowledge_domain: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
story:
Logan ran to the window. "Mom! The sun is out! It is sunny!" He grabbed his sun hat. He wanted to play outside all day.

Then the wind came. It blew his hat right off his head! Logan chased the hat across the grass. The wind was too fast. Mom hung the hat on a hook. "Windy days need a warm jacket," she said, zipping him up.

Then drip, drop, drip. Rain fell on the roof. Logan heard it ping on the pots. He put on his rain boots. He splashed in a big puddle. Splash! Splash! His boots kept his feet dry.

Next, the sky turned white. Snow! Soft flakes landed on his mittens. Logan scooped up snow and patted a little snowman. He put a hat on it too.

Inside, they looked out the window. The sun came back. The little snowman began to melt. It got small, then smaller. "The sun makes it melt because it is warm," said Logan.

His dog barked and shook the snow off his back. Logan yawned a big, sleepy yawn. "One more look," he said. The snowman waved goodbye with one tiny stick arm.
